site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Guha's Lamp by the Ganga
body: At the bank of the Ganga, the chief of the Nishadas, Guha the boatman, welcomed Rama, Sita and Lakshmana with the softest woodsman's care. He spread clean leaf-plates of roots and forest fruit, laid a bed of tender leaves, and kept his lamps burning all night to guard their rest.

He reverently carried the sandals of each one, honoring the prince whose feet had walked so far from Ayodhya. When dawn came and the travelers prepared to continue into exile, Guha's eyes filled with tears he could not hide.

Weeping softly, the hunter asked only to be remembered. Rama placed a gentle hand upon his shoulder and promised he would never be forgotten, leaving Guha with a hope that shone brighter than the vigil lamps he had kept through the dark.

stories.title: A Boy Remembering Vishnu in the Flames
body: In the demon king's palace, the young boy Prahlada would not bow to his father Hiranyakashipu but quietly sang the praises of Narayana among his teachers, his small heart steady with remembrance of Vishnu.

At his father's command, the demon teachers flung Prahlada into a roaring fire and loosed a venomous serpent upon him, yet the flames could not burn and the serpent could not strike a child whose lips still whispered the Lord's name.

When Narayana rose at last from the pillar in the fierce, gentle form of Nrsimha, He lifted Hiranyakashipu onto His lap and turned to the unharmed boy, sending Prahlada forward to rule the demon kingdom in righteousness and without fear.

stories.title: The Lad Who Saved the Serpents
stories.source: Mahabharata — Adi Parva, Astika Parva (Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation)
body: In Hastinapura, King Janamejaya kindled a great fire-sacrifice to avenge his father Parikshit, and serpents were drawn into the flames by the thousand, summoned by the grief he bore for the one called Takshaka who had struck the king down.

From the marriage of the sage Jaratkaru to Vasuki's sister Jaratkaru, a son named Astika had been born, and at last he arrived at the court, praising Janamejaya in verses so wise and gentle that the king, moved, offered him any boon his heart could name.
Astika asked only that the serpents be spared, and Janamejaya kept his word; the fire was quenched, the snake-kind survived, and compassion, speaking through a child, turned wrath into grace.

stories.title: Tara's Plea Before the Trees of Kishkindha
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Kishkindha Kanda, Sarga 18 (Gita Press translation)
body: In the leafy court of Kishkindha, Tara, daughter of the wise physician Sushena, fell at her husband Vali's feet and begged him not to answer Sugriva's challenge for the throne. She had seen how the winds of fortune had shifted and feared what waited in the forest shadows.

She warned that the stranger with the great bow hiding among the branches was no ordinary enemy but Rama of Ayodhya himself, whose friendship with Sugriva had hardened into purpose. Her words, soft and steady, carried the weight of a queen who loved her king more than his pride would allow him to hear.

Vali, swollen with suspicion and the certainty of his own strength, spurned her counsel and strode out to meet his brother. Yet Tara's plea was not lost — for every later telling of the Ramayana holds her up as the honoured voice of reason, a wife's love remembered long after the drums of battle fell silent.

stories.title: Rest and Light at Pampa's Door
body: In the southern wilds where the great search for Sita pressed on, Hanuman came upon a quiet, deserted hermitage. There, fast asleep on a woven mat, lay a young brahmachari — a boy whose lineage entwined the wind-god's sister with the sun-god's son. The stillness of the ashram seemed to wait for a worthy guest.

Gently waking, the radiant boy welcomed Hanuman with warm hospitality, offering divine food drawn from the hermitage's sacred store. As they spoke, the youth unfolded the sorrowful tale of Matanga's curse upon the surrounding forest, and pointed the son of Vayu toward the shining waters of Pampa where his companions waited.

Refreshed in body and heart, Hanuman bowed his thanks and set forth once more across the southern path. The brief kindness of a stranger, offered freely in a lonely place, became the quiet strength that carried his great leap toward hope.
